title: It always takes longer than you expect.
description:
It always takes longer than you expect. Even when you take into account Hofstadter's law. Douglas Hofstadter wrote it in Godel, Escher, Bach in 1979, about chess computers.

Asked 37 psychology students to estimate how long their final year theses would take.

Their average estimate was 33.9 days. The average time they actually took was 55.5 days.

Even the gloomy guess was too short. When asked for a worst case, the average was 48.6 days. That still fell short of the real average.

About this share finished in the time they had predicted.

Add the buffer before you start.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_fallacy: read in full. Established that the planning fallacy was first proposed by Kahneman and Tversky in 1979, and the Buehler, Griffin and Ross study (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 67(3): 366 to 381): 37 psychology students estimating how long their senior theses would take, an average estimate of 33.9 days, a best case average of 27.4, a worst case average of 48.6, an average actual completion of 55.5 days, and about 30 per cent finishing in the time they predicted.
- https://siliconcanals.com/t-productivity-advice-usually-starts-after-the-plan-is-made-but-decades-of-research-suggest-many-missed-deadlines-begin-earlier-with-an-optimistic-estimate-of-how-long-the-work-will-take/: read in full (published 4 August 2026). Corroborated the 33.9 and 55.5 day averages, the roughly 30 per cent figure, and that the average worst case forecast of 48.6 days came in about a week short of the eventual result.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hofstadter%27s_law: read in full. Established the wording of the law, that Douglas Hofstadter introduced it in Godel, Escher, Bach in 1979 in a discussion of chess playing computers, and the Basic Books 1979 page 152 citation.
